45	
46	\paragraph{Why $K{=}4/5$ is the consensus tipping point.}
47	The $K{=}4/5$ threshold reflects the composition of the five-method panel rather than an arbitrary choice.
48	At $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, allowing false positives to pass even when both conservative methods (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto) disagree.
49	At $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, which effectively vetoes spurious signals: null-control FPR drops from 37.5\% to 0\%.
50	Raising the threshold to $K{=}5/5$ requires Toda--Yamamoto agreement, but its low power at $T{=}10$ produces Type~II errors on 3/6 reference pairs (FNR${=}$50\%).
51	The $K{=}4/5$ threshold thus occupies the unique operating point where exactly one low-power method can be excluded without admitting high-FPR coalitions.
52	
53	\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
54	With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
55	This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
56	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
57	This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
58	Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
59	However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
60	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity (3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length), confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.
61	
62	\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
63	Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
64	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
65	In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
66	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
67	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
68	We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.
69	
70	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
71	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
72	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
73	This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.
74	
75	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
76	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
77	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
78	At $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested; at $\alpha{=}0.50$, detectability is seed-dependent (0/8--6/8, 3~seeds, median 3/8), marking the onset boundary where ECE outperforms token entropy as the more sensitive canary.
79	This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
80	At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
81	This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
82	The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track cumulative trend shifts across many generations than to single-point threshold alarms.
83	If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.
84	
85	\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
86	In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
87	A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
88	The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
89	The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.
90	
91	\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
92	In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained Tier~3 agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
93	This complements the continuous monitoring dashboard framing above, where cumulative trend shifts across generations provide more reliable detection than single-point threshold alarms.
94	The cost of running five lightweight statistical tests per generation is negligible relative to the cost of training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) and the absence of intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) mean that such monitoring currently provides diagnostic evidence rather than actionable triggers.
95	
96	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
97	The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
98	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
99	The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
100	In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
101	First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
102	Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.
103	
104	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
105	Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
106	First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
107	This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
108	Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
109	Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
110	Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
111	These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.
112	
113	\paragraph{Future work.}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and five contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds) are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates at these thresholds.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B (single seed each, $\alpha{=}1.0$) replicates the entropy-leads-diversity pattern at Tier~3 consensus: all three model families (Pythia-410M, GPT-2-medium, OPT-1.3B) reach $K{\geq}4/5$ method agreement (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}), with 0 reverse-direction pairs significant across any architecture.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), placing it in the same null/low-detectability regime as Pythia (0/8 Tier~3) and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across two transformer decoder-only model families of similar scale.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger finds 1/8 pairs significant, consistent with its known instability at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).

\paragraph{Why $K{=}4/5$ is the consensus tipping point.}
The $K{=}4/5$ threshold reflects the composition of the five-method panel rather than an arbitrary choice.
At $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, allowing false positives to pass even when both conservative methods (permutation Granger and Toda--Yamamoto) disagree.
At $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, which effectively vetoes spurious signals: null-control FPR drops from 37.5\% to 0\%.
Raising the threshold to $K{=}5/5$ requires Toda--Yamamoto agreement, but its low power at $T{=}10$ produces Type~II errors on 3/6 reference pairs (FNR${=}$50\%).
The $K{=}4/5$ threshold thus occupies the unique operating point where exactly one low-power method can be excluded without admitting high-FPR coalitions.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity (3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length), confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested; at $\alpha{=}0.50$, detectability is seed-dependent (0/8--6/8, 3~seeds, median 3/8), marking the onset boundary where ECE outperforms token entropy as the more sensitive canary.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track cumulative trend shifts across many generations than to single-point threshold alarms.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained Tier~3 agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
This complements the continuous monitoring dashboard framing above, where cumulative trend shifts across generations provide more reliable detection than single-point threshold alarms.
The cost of running five lightweight statistical tests per generation is negligible relative to the cost of training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) and the absence of intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) mean that such monitoring currently provides diagnostic evidence rather than actionable triggers.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the three validated architecture families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT) would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}2$B parameters) remains an open direction.

% [END CONDITIONAL]
Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
Finally, connecting the empirically observed onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$ to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture, Cross-Scale, and Cross-Domain Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

The methodological pitfalls and consensus framework developed above are calibrated on a single model family (Pythia-410M, WikiText-103).
To test whether these findings transfer, we evaluate the consensus pipeline along three generalization axes: architecture family (GPT-2-medium 345M, OPT-1.3B), model scale (Pythia-1.4B, $3.4\times$ parameters within the same family), and training domain (Pythia-1B trained on C4 rather than WikiText-103).

\paragraph{Architecture generalization.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes across all three decoder-only transformer families tested to date.
All models reach Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) with 6/8 (or 6/6) canary$\to$diversity pairs confirmed.
Permutation Granger directionality is perfect across architectures: all forward-direction pairs are FDR-significant while 0 reverse-direction pairs reach significance in any architecture.

Method-level variation across architectures is informative.
Threshold onset detection reaches 8/8 on OPT-1.3B (the highest single-method score) because OPT's token entropy exhibits a pronounced generation-0$\to$1 discontinuity that cleanly exceeds the onset threshold.
Toda--Yamamoto ranges from 0/6 (GPT-2-medium) to 6/8 (Pythia-410M), consistent with its known sensitivity to residual degrees of freedom at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
Despite this cross-method variance, the consensus threshold absorbs it: all three architectures converge at $K{\geq}4/5$.
